source_user: Define KV cache and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: During autoregressive decoding, cached keys and values avoid recomputing prior tokens; memory grows with layers, sequence length, KV heads, head dimension, and bytes per value.
corrected_answer: KV cache stores the attention keys and values produced for tokens that have already been processed, so autoregressive decoding can reuse them instead of recomputing the full prefix at every step. This reduces repeated prefill work and usually improves decode latency, but it consumes GPU memory: for a standard KV layout, storage grows approximately with 2 × layers × sequence_length × KV_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_value. Boundary condition: the cache is per active sequence/request (subject to paging, sharing, or eviction policies), so long contexts and high concurrency can exhaust HBM even when model weights fit.
risks: The memory formula assumes a conventional K/V layout and excludes allocator metadata, padding, quantization effects, and prefix-sharing details.
evidence_required: Confirm formula conventions against the target model architecture and serving engine.

source_user: Define KV cache and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: During autoregressive decoding, cached keys and values avoid recomputing prior tokens; memory grows with layers, sequence length, KV heads, head dimension, and bytes per value.
corrected_answer: The KV cache retains the key and value tensors for previously processed tokens in each attention layer. During the next decode step, attention reads those tensors and computes only the new token's K/V, avoiding recomputation of the prefix. It matters because this can reduce per-token decode computation and latency. Boundary condition: KV-cache memory grows with the number of layers, cached tokens, KV heads, head dimension, and bytes per value, so the benefit is limited by HBM capacity and by the number of concurrent sequences.
risks: Latency benefit depends on implementation and workload; it should not be stated as an unconditional end-to-end SLO improvement.

source_user: Define KV cache and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: During autoregressive decoding, cached keys and values avoid recomputing prior tokens; memory grows with layers, sequence length, KV heads, head dimension, and bytes per value.
corrected_answer: KV cache is the per-sequence storage of attention keys and values from tokens already processed. On each autoregressive step, the new query attends to the cached prefix plus the new K/V, rather than recomputing K/V for every earlier token. This reduces redundant computation during decode. Boundary condition: the cache must remain resident or accessible for the active sequence; if HBM is insufficient, the system may need paging, offload, eviction, or admission control, each of which can change latency and throughput.
risks: Offload and paging behavior is backend-specific and should not be assumed without measurement.

Boundary condition: cache consumption scales with active context and concurrency, and can become the serving bottleneck even if the model weights fit; the exact budget also depends on precision, GQA/MQA layout, padding, and allocator overhead.

source_user: Contrast KV cache with a naive implementation that does not use it. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: During autoregressive decoding, cached keys and values avoid recomputing prior tokens; memory grows with layers, sequence length, KV heads, head dimension, and bytes per value.
corrected_answer: With KV caching, the decoder keeps prior keys and values and computes K/V only for the newly appended token; without it, each decode step recomputes the attention projections for the entire prefix. The cached version therefore trades extra memory for lower repeated compute and usually better decode efficiency. Boundary condition: when cache memory is scarce, paging or offload can add data movement and erase part of the expected latency benefit; a naive no-cache path avoids that memory allocation but scales poorly with context length.
risks: The answer says usually rather than guaranteeing latency improvement because memory traffic and scheduling can dominate.

source_user: Give two failure modes or trade-offs associated with KV cache. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: During autoregressive decoding, cached keys and values avoid recomputing prior tokens; memory grows with layers, sequence length, KV heads, head dimension, and bytes per value.
corrected_answer: Two important trade-offs are: (1) HBM pressure—cache usage grows with active tokens and concurrency, which can cause OOM, admission rejection, eviction, or reduced batch size; and (2) data movement/fragmentation—paging, offload, or fragmented allocations can add latency and reduce effective throughput. Boundary condition: the exact failure point depends on model KV layout, precision, allocator/page size, other resident buffers, and the serving engine, so capacity should be measured with the target workload rather than estimated from weights alone.
risks: OOM and eviction are possible outcomes, not guaranteed; thresholds are deployment-specific.
